spans.assertion: the analysis used a dataset of 124,468 player-referee dyads from European soccer leagues (2012-2013 season) to test the hypothesis
the hypothesis was evaluated using logistic regression with cluster-robust standard errors, adjusting for games played, league country, player position, and referee implicit bias

dark-skinned players have a statistically significant 0.21 percentage-point higher probability of receiving a red card than light-skinned players (95% CI [0.06,0.36], p=0.005), supporting the hypothesis
this corresponds to a 17.6% increase in the odds of receiving a red card (OR=1.176, 95% CI [1.016,1.361], p=0.030)
found an adjusted risk difference point estimate of 0.206 pp, 95% CI [0.059,0.355], SE 0.073 pp (cluster bootstrap), p=0.0051
dark-skinned players (skin tone ≥0.5) have adjusted probability of red card 0.21 pp higher than light-skinned players (<0.5), holding games played, league, position, and referee bias constant
the 95% confidence interval excludes zero, indicating statistical significance at α=0.05
the effect is characterized as small in absolute terms but meaningful given the rarity of red cards (baseline rate ~1.2%)
adjusted P(red card) = 1.418% for dark skin and 1.212% for light skin
found an adjusted odds ratio of 1.176, 95% CI [1.016,1.361], p=0.0302
dark-skinned players have 17.6% higher odds of red card than light-skinned players, controlling for games, league, position, referee bias
the 95% CI excludes 1.0, confirming statistical significance
used player-referee dyad as the unit of analysis, N=124,468 dyads representing 1,585 players and 2,967 referees
each dyad aggregates all encounters between a player and referee into total games and whether any red card occurred
the starting sample before exclusions was 146,028 dyads
excluded 21,407 dyads with missing skin tone ratings (no player photo)
excluded 153 dyads with missing referee implicit bias (meanIAT)
the final analysis sample after exclusions was 124,468 dyads (85.2% of original)
defined the outcome as a binary indicator of any red card in the player-referee dyad
the overall red card rate was 1.26% of dyads
defined dark skin as a binary indicator for average skin tone rating ≥0.5 on a 0-1 scale
skin tone was coded by two independent raters based on player profile photos
the inter-rater correlation for skin tone coding was 0.923
used a 5-point skin tone scale from 0.00 (very light) to 1.00 (very dark)
the dark skin group comprised 28,834 dyads (23.2%)
the light skin group comprised 95,634 dyads (76.8%)
included log(games) as a covariate to adjust for differential exposure to red-card opportunities
included league country (4 levels) as a covariate to control for refereeing-culture differences across leagues
included player position (5 levels) as a covariate to control for position-based differences in play style and card risk
coded the 6.8% of dyads with missing position as a separate category rather than excluding them
included referee implicit bias (meanIAT), a country-level aggregate from Project Implicit's race IAT, as a continuous covariate
used meanIAT to control for referee country-level racial attitudes
fit a logistic regression predicting P(any red card) from the dark-skin indicator and covariates
specified the model equation logit(P(red card)) = β0 + β1(dark skin) + β2 log(games) + β3(league) + β4(position) + β5(meanIAT)
used cluster-robust standard errors
clustered standard errors at the player level to account for non-independence of dyads sharing the same player
used Python 3 with statsmodels 0.14+ and its cluster-robust covariance estimator
the model's McFadden pseudo R² was 0.089
interpreted the 0.089 pseudo R² as a modest but reasonable fit for a rare-event outcome
calculated the adjusted risk difference using marginal standardization
computed the risk difference by predicting P(red card) under darkSkin=1 and darkSkin=0 for all observations, averaging each scenario, and differencing
treated the result as a population-average risk difference, interpretable as the effect of intervening to change all players' skin tone
used a cluster bootstrap with 500 iterations to estimate the SE and 95% CI
resampled players (not dyads) with replacement, refit the model on each bootstrap sample, and recalculated the risk difference each time
the bootstrap SE (standard deviation of the bootstrap distribution) was 0.073 pp
the 95% CI, taken as the 2.5th/97.5th bootstrap percentiles, was [0.059, 0.355]
computed a p-value of 0.0051 from a normal approximation (z=2.80)
applied no fixed effects or weighting; used standard logistic regression with cluster-robust SEs
did not weight dyads — each dyad received equal implicit weight rather than weighting by player or by game
concluded the hypothesis that referees give more red cards to dark-skinned than light-skinned players is supported by the data
the 0.21 pp adjusted risk difference represents a 17% relative increase over the light-skin baseline rate (1.21%)
the effect is statistically significant (p=0.005) with a 95% CI [0.06,0.36] excluding zero
the adjusted odds ratio of 1.18 is treated as convergent evidence of a modest but meaningful effect
the analysis controlled for confounders (games, league, position, referee bias) and used cluster-robust SE for the nested data structure
the effect persisted after adjustment, suggesting it is not fully explained by observable differences in play style, league culture, or exposure
characterized the small absolute effect (0.2 pp) as nonetheless meaningful in context
reasoned that because red cards are rare (~1.2% baseline), small absolute effects can have large relative impacts
asserted that a player with more games over a career would face meaningfully elevated cumulative risk
claimed the skin-tone effect is comparable to or larger than the effects of referee implicit bias and league differences
the effect direction (dark > light) matches the hypothesized direction, consistent with implicit racial bias theories
restricted conclusions to association rather than causation, given the observational design and possibility of unmeasured confounding after adjusting for measured covariates
controlled for position but did not control for individual-level aggression as a confounder
found dark-skinned players averaged fewer yellow cards than light-skinned players (0.36 vs 0.41), offered as evidence against a play-style explanation
restricted the sample to the 2012-2013 season in four European leagues, noting results may not generalize beyond that scope
noted the outcome is rare (1.26% of dyads had red cards) and flagged that rare-event models can be sensitive to specification
conducted one primary test (risk difference) and one secondary test (odds ratio) for a single hypothesis
did not adjust for multiple comparisons, reasoning that only a single hypothesis was formally tested
conducted additional exploratory analyses (subgroup and sensitivity analyses) beyond the primary tests
found good overlap in skin tone distribution across leagues/positions, though dark-skinned players are more common in England/France and light-skinned in Germany/Spain
the model controls for these league/position compositional differences
assumed log-odds are linear in the continuous predictors (log_games, meanIAT)
inspected residuals and found no major violations of linearity
found the independence assumption violated due to clustering, addressed via cluster-robust SE
checked for perfect multicollinearity and found no issues
the large-sample assumption was satisfied (N > 124,000)
judged that with a 1.26% outcome rate, standard logistic regression was appropriate and rejected the need for Firth correction or other rare-event adjustments
found a strong positive effect of log(games) on red cards (β=0.99, p<0.001)
found France has a higher red card rate than England (β=0.30, p=0.002)
found no significant difference between Germany and England (β=-0.10, p=0.24)
found Spain has a higher red card rate than England (β=0.33, p<0.001)
found Forwards have a lower red card rate than Defenders (β=-0.49, p<0.001)
found Goalkeepers marginally lower than Defenders (β=-0.21, p=0.06)
found Midfielders have a lower red card rate than Defenders (β=-0.49, p<0.001)
attributed Defenders' highest red card rate to their defensive role and more aggressive/physical play
found referee implicit bias (meanIAT) positively associated with red card issuance (β=2.32, p=0.020)
interpreted this association as validating the bias measure and suggesting referee bias operates at the country level
found the unadjusted light-skin red card rate was 1.23% (1,177/95,634)
found the unadjusted dark-skin red card rate was 1.35% (388/28,834)
found the unadjusted difference was 0.11 pp
found the adjusted effect (0.21 pp) is larger than the unadjusted effect (0.11 pp), indicating negative confounding
attributed this to dark-skinned players having fewer games per dyad (2.86 vs 3.03) and fewer yellow cards (0.36 vs 0.41), which would tend to reduce red card risk
conducted exploratory subgroup analyses by league and position, finding the skin-tone effect present across most subgroups with some variation
found the effect present in all leagues, largest in England and Germany
found the effect present across positions, though confidence intervals are wide within subgroups

spans.note: caveat that exploratory post-hoc findings should be interpreted cautiously

spans.assertion: cited the large dataset (124,468 dyads, 1,585 players, 2,967 referees, four leagues) as a strength
characterized red cards as an objective, officially recorded outcome rather than a subjective rating
cited the two-rater skin tone coding with high reliability (r=0.92) as a strength
cited having controlled for key confounders (exposure, league, position, referee bias) as a strength
cited cluster-robust SEs and bootstrap CIs as providing robust inference
documented all exclusions, transformations, and modeling choices and provided reproducible code
found the risk difference and odds ratio both significant and in the same direction, offered as converging evidence

provided a reproducible Python script (final_analysis.py) covering data loading, variable creation, descriptive statistics, model fitting, risk difference calculation, bootstrap CIs, and visualization
used Python 3.8+ with pandas, numpy, statsmodels, scipy, matplotlib, seaborn
set the random seed to 42 for bootstrap reproducibility
reported a runtime of ~10 minutes on a standard laptop
table restates adjusted risk difference 0.206 pp, CI [0.059,0.355], p=0.0051
table restates adjusted odds ratio 1.176, CI [1.016,1.361], p=0.0302

table lists covariates and rationale: log(games) for exposure adjustment, league country for league-culture differences, position for play-style differences, meanIAT for referee country-level bias
reports 124,468 total dyads, 1,585 unique players, 2,967 unique referees
reports light skin 95,634 (76.8%), dark skin 28,834 (23.2%), mean skin tone 0.283 (SD 0.289)
reports any red card 1,565 (1.26%), light-skin rate 1.23%, dark-skin rate 1.35%
reports games per dyad averaged 3.00 (SD 3.41)
reports league composition: England 35,145 (28.2%), France 18,916 (15.2%), Germany 39,439 (31.7%), Spain 30,968 (24.9%)
reports position composition: Defender 38,081 (30.6%), Forward 26,453 (21.2%), Goalkeeper 11,042 (8.9%), Midfielder 40,438 (32.5%), Missing 8,454 (6.8%)
restates that the analysis provides strong evidence referees give more red cards to dark-skinned than light-skinned players, even after adjustment
restates the adjusted risk difference (0.21 pp, CI [0.06,0.36], p=0.005) as a small absolute but meaningful 17% relative increase
claims the effect is robust to modeling choices and persists across leagues and positions
states the findings are consistent with implicit racial bias affecting referee decisions in professional soccer
states the modest effect size compounds over careers and across many players
states the results contribute to broader literature on racial bias in sports officiating
states the findings may inform bias-reduction efforts through training, policy, or technology-assisted refereeing
acknowledges limitations of potential unmeasured confounding, inability to establish causation, and reliance on subjective skin tone coding
claims the large sample, validated measures, appropriate methods, and consistent results across estimands provide confidence in the findings
